\chapter{Five Last Pieces}
\label{ch:piezas-sueltas}
\hlchaptermodality{428}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read an e-mail address aloud with every symbol named, congratulate somebody, raise a glass, answer a sneeze, and name a creature I do not have the word for.}

Read an invitation with an address on it, saying each symbol by name, and answer it with the right word at each moment of the evening.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la arroba]{la arroba — Spanish has a word where English has a noise}

\label{lesson:ES-C428-arroba}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el correo electrónico}. Now try to say your e-mail address aloud in Spanish, and stop at the symbol in the middle.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la arroba} — the \textbf{@} sign.

English calls it \emph{at}, which is a preposition pressed into service. Spanish has a \textbf{noun} for it, and the noun is much older than e-mail.

An \emph{arroba} was a unit of weight — about eleven and a half kilos — from Arabic \textbf{ar-rubʿ}, \textquotedblleft{}the quarter,\textquotedblright{} because it was a quarter of a \emph{quintal}. Merchants wrote it with a looped \textbf{a}, and that shorthand is the symbol on your keyboard.

So when a Spanish speaker reads out an address, they are naming a \textbf{medieval unit of weight}:

\begin{quote}
ana \textbf{arroba} ejemplo punto es
\end{quote}

You have the other two pieces already: \textbf{punto} for the dot, from the punctuation chapter, and \textbf{guion} if the address carries one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: reading an address aloud}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{symbol} & \textbf{said aloud} \\
\midrule
@ & arroba \\
. & punto \\
- & guion \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A listening paper dictates an address using exactly these words, and the whole task is unreadable without the first one. Note that the symbol is \textbf{feminine}: \emph{la arroba}, because the unit of weight was.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la arroba\textquotedblright{}
  \item what an \emph{arroba} was before it was a symbol
  \item your own e-mail address aloud, in Spanish
  \item the three symbols and their Spanish names
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was an \emph{arroba} originally? (A unit of weight, a quarter of a \emph{quintal}.) Which article does it take? (\emph{La}.) What does a Spanish speaker say where an English speaker says \textquotedblleft{}at\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Arroba}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el guion bajo]{el guion bajo — the hyphen that sits on the floor}

\label{lesson:ES-C428-guion-bajo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el guion}, the short mark that joins. Say \emph{la arroba}. One symbol remains before an address can be read out complete.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el guion bajo} — the underscore, \textbf{\_}.

The name is transparent and worth admiring for it: \emph{guion} is the hyphen you already know, and \textbf{bajo} means \emph{low}. It is the \textbf{low hyphen} — the same mark, dropped to the baseline.

English names it \emph{under-score}, from the typewriter habit of scoring a line \emph{under} text to underline it. Spanish names it by where it sits relative to the mark it resembles. Two languages, two entirely reasonable descriptions of the same key.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the address, complete}]
Every symbol an e-mail address can contain now has a Spanish name:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{symbol} & \textbf{said aloud} \\
\midrule
@ & arroba \\
. & punto \\
- & guion \\
\_ & guion bajo \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
ana\_lopez \textbf{arroba} ejemplo \textbf{punto} es
\end{quote}

Read that aloud and you have completed the task the source calls \emph{dictating an e-mail address}. It needed four words, three of which you already had.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el guion bajo\textquotedblright{}, and say what \emph{bajo} is telling you
  \item the four symbol names in order
  \item the address above, aloud and complete
  \item the difference between \emph{guion} and \emph{guion bajo} on the page
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{bajo} mean? (Low.) So what is a \emph{guion bajo}? (A low hyphen — the underscore.) How many of the four address symbols did you already have before this chapter? (Three.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¡Felicidades!]{¡Felicidades! — the word you say, not the word you describe with}

\label{lesson:ES-C428-felicidades}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el guion bajo}. The symbols are finished; what follows is what you say to people. Say \emph{feliz}, then try to congratulate somebody with it — and notice the adjective will not do it.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{¡Felicidades!} — \textquotedblleft{}congratulations.\textquotedblright{}

It is \emph{felicidad}, \textquotedblleft{}happiness,\textquotedblright{} in the \textbf{plural} — literally \emph{happinesses}. Spanish wishes several at once, which is what a congratulation is: not a description of a state but a handful of good wishes thrown at somebody.

The relationship to \emph{feliz} is visible: \emph{feliz} $\to$ \emph{felicidad} $\to$ \emph{felicidades}. An adjective, the noun made from it, and that noun pluralised into an act.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which one on which occasion}]
Spanish has two congratulation words and they are not interchangeable:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{for} \\
\midrule
\textbf{¡Felicidades!} & a birthday, a saint's day, a wedding — an \textbf{occasion} \\
¡Felicitaciones! & an exam passed, a job won — an \textbf{achievement} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Felicidades} is the one an A1 paper wants, because A1 life is birthdays rather than promotions. In much of Latin America \emph{felicitaciones} is the commoner of the two; in Spain \emph{felicidades} covers nearly everything.

And note the marks: an exclamation in Spanish opens with \textbf{¡} and closes with \textbf{!}, the same doubling you learned for questions.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¡Felicidades!\textquotedblright{}
  \item the singular noun it is built from (\emph{felicidad})
  \item the adjective under that (\emph{feliz})
  \item which of the two congratulation words fits a birthday
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{¡Felicidades!} literally say? (\emph{Happinesses} — several at once.) Which word suits an achievement rather than an occasion? (\emph{¡Felicitaciones!})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¡Salud!]{¡Salud! — a noun doing a job}

\label{lesson:ES-C428-salud-brindis}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la salud}, health. Say \emph{¡Felicidades!} You have one noun that describes and one that acts. This lesson turns the first into the second.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{¡Salud!} — \textquotedblleft{}cheers,\textquotedblright{} raising a glass.

It is the same word you already have, with no article and an exclamation around it. Stripped of \emph{la}, it stops describing a condition and becomes a \textbf{wish}: \emph{health to you}.

That is what almost every toast in Europe is. English \emph{cheers} wishes cheerfulness; Irish \emph{sláinte} is literally \emph{health}; and \emph{¡Salud!} is the Spanish member of the same family. Raising a glass is wishing somebody well, and most languages say so plainly.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same word, two occasions}]
\textbf{¡Salud!} does a second job that catches English speakers out:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{when} & \textbf{what it means} \\
\midrule
raising a glass & cheers \\
after somebody sneezes & bless you \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English uses two unrelated expressions for those. Spanish uses one word for both, and the reason is the same in each case: \textbf{you are wishing the person health}, whether because they are about to drink or because they have sneezed.

Some speakers say \emph{¡Jesús!} after a sneeze instead, and in a formal toast you may hear the fuller \emph{¡A tu salud!} — \textquotedblleft{}to your health.\textquotedblright{} The bare word covers both occasions and is never wrong.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¡Salud!\textquotedblright{} with no article
  \item the two occasions it fits
  \item \emph{la salud} and \emph{¡Salud!} one after the other, and name the difference
  \item which one you would use at a birthday alongside \emph{¡Felicidades!}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the difference on the page between the noun and the toast? (The article — the toast drops it.) What are the two occasions for \emph{¡Salud!}? (Raising a glass, and after a sneeze.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el animal]{el animal — a thing with breath in it}

\label{lesson:ES-C428-animal}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{¡Salud!} — a word you already had, put to a new use. Now name three creatures you can say in Spanish, and try to say the word that covers all three at once.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el animal} — \textquotedblleft{}the animal.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{animal}, from \textbf{anima}, \textquotedblleft{}breath, soul.\textquotedblright{} An animal is literally \textbf{a thing that has breath in it} — which is how Latin drew the line between the living and the not-living, at the lungs.

\emph{Anima} is generous, and every word on it is about that breath:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the breath in it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{anim}al & a thing that breathes \\
\textbf{ánim}o & spirit, courage \\
des\textbf{anim}ado & discouraged — the breath gone out \\
re\textbf{anim}ar & to revive — to put the breath back \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English took the same root for \textbf{animate}, \textbf{unanimous} (of one \emph{anima}, one mind) and \textbf{magnanimous} (of a great one).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the word that covers the others}]
This is a \textbf{superordinate} — a word one level up from the ones it covers. The corpus has taught particular creatures for hundreds of chapters without ever teaching the category they belong to.

That gap matters more than it looks. A superordinate is what lets you talk about something you cannot name: \emph{un animal grande} works when you do not know the word for the creature in front of you, and a reading paper will use it exactly that way, in a notice or a sign that must cover every creature at once.

The stress is on the last syllable — \emph{a-ni-MAL} — and there is no written accent, because a word ending in \textbf{-l} is stressed there by default.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el animal\textquotedblright{} — \emph{a-ni-MAL}
  \item what \emph{anima} meant, and where Latin drew the line
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un animal grande\textquotedblright{}, and say when you would need it
  \item which English word means \textquotedblleft{}of one mind\textquotedblright{} and hides the same root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{anima} mean? (Breath, soul.) Why does \emph{animal} carry no written accent? (A word ending in \textbf{-l} is stressed on the last syllable anyway.) What is a superordinate for? (Talking about a thing you cannot name.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cinco piezas sueltas]{cinco piezas sueltas — five things that finish five different jobs}

\label{lesson:ES-C428-repaso-cortesia}



\begin{quote}
Name the five before reading the table. They have less in common than usual, which is the point.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what each one completes}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{finishes} \\
\midrule
la arroba & reading an address aloud \\
el guion bajo & the same \\
¡Felicidades! & congratulating somebody \\
¡Salud! & raising a glass, and answering a sneeze \\
el animal & naming a creature you cannot name \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The address needed only these two: \emph{punto} and \emph{guion} were already yours from the punctuation chapter.

Each was the \textbf{last missing piece} of something the corpus could otherwise nearly do. That is what makes them worth a chapter together despite having nothing else in common: the address needed two more words, the social phrases were absent although the adjectives behind them were taught, and a dozen creatures had no category.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two of them are nouns doing other work}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{as a noun} & \textbf{as an act} \\
\midrule
salud & health & cheers, bless you \\
felicidad & happiness & — \\
felicidades & — & congratulations \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{¡Salud!} drops its article and becomes a wish. \textbf{¡Felicidades!} takes a plural and becomes an act. Neither is a new word in the ordinary sense; both are an existing word put to a different use, which is why the adjectives behind them were never enough on their own.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two symbol names, and the two you already had
  \item the two things you say to people, and the occasion for each
  \item what a superordinate is for
  \item what happens to \emph{salud} when it loses its article
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two of the five are existing words put to a new use? (\emph{Salud} and \emph{felicidades}.) What was an \emph{arroba} before it was a symbol? (A unit of weight.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[una invitación]{una invitación — reading it, and answering it}

\label{lesson:ES-C428-sintesis-cumpleanos}



\begin{quote}
Say the two things you would say at a birthday. One congratulates and one raises a glass.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Read this invitation aloud, saying every symbol by name:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Cumpleaños de Ana} Sábado, a las ocho. Confirma en ana\_lopez arroba ejemplo punto es
\end{quote}

The address line is written in words here because that is how it is \textbf{said}. On a screen it would read \emph{ana\_lopez@ejemplo.es}, and saying it aloud requires the four names: \emph{guion bajo}, \emph{arroba}, \emph{punto}, and the letters themselves.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: answering it}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{moment} & \textbf{what you say} \\
\midrule
arriving & ¡Felicidades! \\
the first glass & ¡Salud! \\
somebody sneezes & ¡Salud! \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two words cover the whole evening, and one of them covers two of the three moments.

If the invitation had been to a farm rather than a flat, you would also have the word for whatever was in the field: \emph{un animal}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the address line aloud, every symbol by name
  \item what you say on arriving, and what you say at the first glass
  \item the same word again, this time because somebody sneezed
  \item your own e-mail address aloud in Spanish
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many symbol names does reading an address aloud need? (Four.) Which of the two social words covers two different moments? (\emph{¡Salud!})
\end{tcolorbox}
